cards.explanation: The answer is the Lord. Verse 2 says it plainly: “…the Lord delivered into his hand Jehoiakim king of Judah…” Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is the one who came to Jerusalem and besieged it (Daniel 1:1). Still, the text names the Lord as the One who delivered. It's a heavy verse, friends, so I'm not going to joke over it.

The answer is to serve in the king's palace. Verse 4 says these young men are “…qualified to serve in the king’s palace…” Handsome, gifted and quick to understand, that's the résumé the king asks for. And he asks for all of it at once, friends. Nobody gets to pick just one.

The answer is language. Verse 4 says Ashpenaz is to teach them “…the language and literature of the Chaldeans.” Language comes first, which makes sense when you're going to work in a foreign palace. Showing up and not understanding a word anybody says would make for a long first week. I've had days like that in a junk drawer, and nobody was even talking.

The answer is True. Verse 5 says “They were to be trained for three years, after which they were to enter the king’s service.” Three years is a long time to be in training. That's more than a few batches of cookies, friends. The king was not rushing this.

The answer is new names. Verse 7 says the chief official gave them new names. Daniel became Belteshazzar, Hananiah became Shadrach, Mishael became Meshach and Azariah became Abednego. Four young men and four brand new names in one verse. I'd need a minute just to learn how to sign them.

The answer is False. Daniel does not go straight to the king. Verse 8 says Daniel “…asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.” He starts with the chief official. Walking up to the king himself would be a much louder move, friends.

The answer is thinner faces than the others. The chief official says, “For why should he see your faces looking thinner than those of the other young men your age?” He's thinking about what the king will see when he looks at their faces. I think he's nervous, friends. Nobody wants to be the one explaining skinny faces to a king.

The answer is True. The chief official says it straight: “You would endanger my head before the king!” He's not worried about a scolding, friends. He's talking about his own head. I think he really did not want this to go sideways.

The answer is only vegetables and water. Daniel asks, “Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink.” That's the whole menu he puts on the table, and he asks for just ten days of it. Picture that request landing at a king's table, friends. I'd have asked for a cookie on the side.

The answer is compare. Daniel says, “…compare our appearances with those of the young men who are eating the royal food, and deal with your servants according to what you see.” Compare is the word he picks. He's not asking the steward to take his word for it. He lets the steward look and decide, and I admire that, friends.

The answer is False. The four do not look thinner. Verse 15 says “…they looked healthier and better nourished than all the young men who were eating the king’s food.” That's the opposite of what the chief official feared in verse 10. I bet that surprised somebody.

The answer is that he keeps giving them vegetables instead. Verse 16 says “…the steward continued to withhold their choice food and the wine they were to drink, and he gave them vegetables instead.” The test ended and the vegetables kept coming. When something works, friends, you don't touch it. I'd do the same with my best cookie recipe.

The answer is all kinds of visions and dreams. Verse 17 says, “And Daniel had insight into all kinds of visions and dreams.” The four got knowledge and understanding in every kind of literature and wisdom. Then Daniel gets this extra, friends. That's a gift on top of a gift.

The answer is True. Verse 19 says the king spoke with them, “…and among all the young men he found no one equal to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.” Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, looked at the whole group and found no one equal to these four. Then they entered the king's service. Three years of training, and these four came out on top.

The answer is ten times better than all of them. Verse 20 says the king “…found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.” Ten times, friends, and not just better than the average one. That's better than all of them. Let that sit for a second.
